title: About this portfolio
text:
This website is my learning portfolio for ISSS608 Visual Analytics and Applications. It records the methods, code, visualisations, and interpretations developed through the course’s hands-on exercises.
The portfolio is created with R and Quarto, version-controlled on GitHub, and published as a website through Vercel.

title: About this portfolio
text:
Course themes

Geospatial data import, transformation, and geoprocessing
Thematic mapping and geovisualisation
First- and second-order spatial point-pattern analysis
Spatio-temporal point-pattern analysis

The worked pages are organised under the Hands-on Exercises dropdown in the navigation bar.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1
text:
This exercise follows Chapter 1: Geospatial Data Science with R. It demonstrates how to import, inspect, project, convert, and geoprocess spatial data in R. The analysis answers two practical questions:

How much land lies within five metres of Singapore’s cycling-path network?
How are pre-schools distributed across Master Plan 2014 subzones?

title: Hands-on Exercise 1
text:
Data and packages
The current data.gov.sg downloads are GeoJSON rather than the shapefile and KML formats used in the original course notes. GeoJSON is used here because it is the current official downloadable format and preserves the geometry in one file.
The requested Master Plan 2014 Subzone Boundary (Web) collection currently has no downloadable child dataset. I therefore use Master Plan 2014 Subzone Boundary (No Sea). This substitution is appropriate for area-based pre-school density because offshore polygons would enlarge coastal subzones without adding pre-schools.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1
text:
Importing geospatial data
st_read() reads all three vector datasets as simple-feature data frames. The course’s chap01/data/... path belongs to the lecturer’s project; the paths below match this repository.


Show the R code
mpsz <- st_read(
  file.path(data_path, "geospatial", "MasterPlan2014SubzoneBoundaryNoSea.geojson"),
  quiet = TRUE
)

cyclingpath <- st_read(
  file.path(data_path, "geospatial", "CyclingPathNetwork.geojson"),
  quiet = TRUE
)

preschool <- st_read(
  file.path(data_path, "geospatial", "PreSchoolsLocation.geojson"),
  quiet = TRUE
)



Inspecting the feature data frames
Before analysing the data, I check the number of features, geometry type, attributes, and coordinate reference system (CRS).


Show the R code
spatial_summary <- data.frame(
  Object = c("Planning subzones", "Cycling paths", "Pre-schools"),
  Features = c(nrow(mpsz), nrow(cyclingpath), nrow(preschool)),
  Attributes = c(ncol(mpsz) - 1, ncol(cyclingpath) - 1, ncol(preschool) - 1),
  Geometry = c(
    paste(unique(as.character(st_geometry_type(mpsz))), collapse = ", "),
    paste(unique(as.character(st_geometry_type(cyclingpath))), collapse = ", "),
    paste(unique(as.character(st_geometry_type(preschool))), collapse = ", ")
  ),
  `Native CRS` = c(st_crs(mpsz)$input, st_crs(cyclingpath)$input, st_crs(preschool)$input),
  check.names = FALSE
)

kable(spatial_summary, caption = "Imported geospatial datasets")

title: Hands-on Exercise 1
text:
Working with projection
Distance and area should not be calculated in longitude and latitude. I transform all three objects to SVY21 / Singapore TM (EPSG:3414), a projected CRS measured in metres.


Show the R code
mpsz <- st_transform(mpsz, crs = 3414)
cyclingpath <- st_transform(cyclingpath, crs = 3414)
preschool <- st_transform(preschool, crs = 3414)

crs_check <- data.frame(
  Object = c("Planning subzones", "Cycling paths", "Pre-schools"),
  EPSG = c(st_crs(mpsz)$epsg, st_crs(cyclingpath)$epsg, st_crs(preschool)$epsg),
  Units = c("metres", "metres", "metres")
)

kable(crs_check, caption = "CRS after transformation")

title: Hands-on Exercise 1
text:
Importing and converting aspatial data
The Airbnb CSV contains longitude and latitude fields but no geometry column, so it begins as an ordinary data frame.


Show the R code
listings <- read.csv(
  file.path(data_path, "aspatial", "listings.csv"),
  check.names = FALSE
)

listings_sf <- st_as_sf(
  listings,
  coords = c("longitude", "latitude"),
  crs = 4326,
  remove = FALSE
) |>
  st_transform(crs = 3414)

listing_summary <- data.frame(
  Records = nrow(listings_sf),
  Geometry = paste(unique(as.character(st_geometry_type(listings_sf))), collapse = ", "),
  EPSG = st_crs(listings_sf)$epsg,
  `Longitude/latitude retained` = all(c("longitude", "latitude") %in% names(listings_sf)),
  check.names = FALSE
)

kable(listing_summary, caption = "Airbnb data after conversion to a spatial object")

The coordinate order is longitude, latitude (x, y). Reversing it would place the observations far outside Singapore. The converted object contains 3,447 point features in EPSG:3414.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1
text:
Geoprocessing

Question 1: How much land is within 5 m of a cycling path?
A five-metre buffer is created on both sides of every cycling-path feature. Summing the separate buffer areas double-counts overlaps, so I also dissolve the buffers with st_union() to obtain the unique footprint.


Show the R code
buffer_cycling <- st_buffer(cyclingpath, dist = 5, nQuadSegs = 30)

naive_buffer_ha <- st_area(buffer_cycling) |>
  sum() |>
  set_units("ha")

dissolved_buffer_ha <- buffer_cycling |>
  st_union() |>
  st_area() |>
  set_units("ha")

overlap_pct <- as.numeric(
  (naive_buffer_ha - dissolved_buffer_ha) / naive_buffer_ha * 100
)

buffer_results <- data.frame(
  Method = c("Sum of individual buffers", "Dissolved unique footprint"),
  `Area (hectares)` = round(c(as.numeric(naive_buffer_ha), as.numeric(dissolved_buffer_ha)), 2),
  check.names = FALSE
)

kable(buffer_results, caption = "Area within five metres of cycling paths")



Area within five metres of cycling paths


Method
Area (hectares)




Sum of individual buffers
498.97


Dissolved unique footprint
431.51





Answer. The non-overlapping five-metre buffer covers approximately 431.51 hectares. A simple sum gives 498.97 hectares because overlapping buffers are counted more than once, overstating the unique footprint by about 13.5%.


Question 2: How many pre-schools are in each subzone?
st_intersects() returns the pre-school row indices that fall inside each subzone. lengths() converts that list into one count per subzone.


Show the R code
mpsz$PreSch_Count <- lengths(st_intersects(mpsz, preschool))

top_count <- mpsz |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  select(SUBZONE_N, PLN_AREA_N, PreSch_Count) |>
  arrange(desc(PreSch_Count)) |>
  head(10)

kable(
  top_count,
  col.names = c("Subzone", "Planning area", "Pre-schools"),
  caption = "Subzones with the most pre-schools"
)

Pre-school density
Counts favour large residential subzones. Dividing by area shows the number of pre-schools per square kilometre and provides a different view of provision.


Show the R code
mpsz$Area_sqkm <- st_area(mpsz) |>
  set_units("km^2") |>
  as.numeric()

mpsz$PreSch_Density <- mpsz$PreSch_Count / mpsz$Area_sqkm

top_density <- mpsz |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  select(SUBZONE_N, PreSch_Count, Area_sqkm, PreSch_Density) |>
  arrange(desc(PreSch_Density)) |>
  head(10) |>
  mutate(
    Area_sqkm = round(Area_sqkm, 2),
    PreSch_Density = round(PreSch_Density, 2)
  )

kable(
  top_density,
  col.names = c("Subzone", "Pre-schools", "Area (km²)", "Pre-schools per km²"),
  caption = "Subzones with the highest pre-school density"
)

CECIL has the highest density at 35.6 pre-schools per km². This does not mean it has the most facilities: small-area subzones can rank highly even with modest counts. Count is more useful for absolute provision, while density is more useful for provision relative to land area.

  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "C", name = "Count") +
  labs(title = "Pre-school count by subzone") +

title: Hands-on Exercise 1
text:
Exploratory data analysis


Show the R code
ggplot(mpsz, aes(x = PreSch_Density)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = "#4f86c6", color = "white") +
  labs(
    title = "Pre-school density is strongly right-skewed",
    subtitle = "Most subzones have low density; a small number have high values",
    x = "Pre-schools per square kilometre",
    y = "Number of subzones"
  )





Distribution of pre-school density across subzones




The long right tail confirms that most subzones have few pre-schools per square kilometre and a small number have much higher density. This matters for later thematic mapping because different classification methods can present a skewed variable very differently.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1
text:
Key findings

The current official spatial files contain 323 subzones, 8,523 cycling-path features, and 2,290 pre-school locations.
Transforming from WGS84 to EPSG:3414 is essential before calculating metres or square kilometres.
The unique five-metre cycling-path buffer covers about 431.51 hectares.
TAMPINES EAST has the most pre-schools (72), while CECIL has the highest density (35.6 per km²).
Count and density answer different questions, and density is sensitive to very small subzone areas.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1
text:
Limitations
The datasets come from different reference dates, so the analysis is a methodological exercise rather than a fully time-aligned planning study. A five-metre buffer measures geometric proximity, not construction feasibility or legal land acquisition. Density per land area also does not account for the number or age of children living in each subzone.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5
text: This exercise examines whether point events interact across a range of distances and whether the observed pattern is more clustered or dispersed than an appropriate reference process.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5
text:
Learning focus

Prepare spatial point-pattern data and a valid observation window.
Use the G-function to study nearest-event distances.
Use the F-function to study empty-space distances.
Use K- and L-functions to assess spatial dependence across distances.
Compare observed statistics with simulation envelopes.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5
text:
Analysis workflow

Import and validate the study-area and event data.
Convert the data into the structures required for point-pattern analysis.
Define a suitable null model and simulation settings.
Compute G-, F-, K-, and L-function diagnostics.
Interpret departures from the simulation envelope carefully and in context.







Conclusions depend on the observation window, edge correction, distance range, and reference process used.

title: Hands-on Exercise 4
text: This exercise studies the intensity and broad spatial distribution of point events using nearest-neighbour methods and kernel density estimation (KDE).

title: Hands-on Exercise 4
text:
Learning focus

Import, wrangle, and validate event and study-area data.
Prepare point-pattern objects for analysis.
Apply the Clark–Evans nearest-neighbour test.
Estimate spatial intensity with kernel density estimation.
Compare fixed and adaptive bandwidth approaches.
Produce a cartographically clear KDE map.
Summarise first-order patterns at planning-subzone level.

title: Hands-on Exercise 4
text:
Analysis workflow

Define the study area and clean the point-event data.
Confirm that the coordinate system is suitable for distance-based analysis.
Examine nearest-neighbour structure.
Estimate and compare density surfaces.
Interpret where event intensity is relatively high or low, with attention to boundary effects and bandwidth choice.







First-order methods describe intensity across space; they do not by themselves establish why a pattern occurs.

title: Hands-on Exercise 2
text: This exercise develops clear thematic maps from geospatial data and explores how classification, symbols, layout, and interactivity affect what a map communicates.

title: Hands-on Exercise 2
text:
Learning focus

Import and prepare the required spatial and attribute data.
Build choropleth maps with tmap.
Compare variables through small-multiple maps.
Highlight spatial features that meet a selection criterion.
Combine thematic maps with statistical charts.
Create an interactive map for exploration.

title: Hands-on Exercise 2
text:
Analysis workflow

Check the spatial data, attributes, and coordinate reference system.
Select a meaningful variable and appropriate classification method.
Design a readable static thematic map with suitable labels and legend.
Compare patterns with small multiples or a supporting chart.
Add interactivity where it improves exploration of the data.







Map design choices should be justified by the analytical question, not only by visual appearance.

title: Hands-on Exercise 6
text: This exercise extends point-pattern analysis into time, showing how the location and intensity of events evolve across temporal intervals.

title: Hands-on Exercise 6
text:
Learning focus

Prepare a study area and event data with valid spatial and temporal fields.
Visualise point events across time.
Compute spatio-temporal kernel density estimates by month and day of year.
Compare alternative approaches to temporal grouping and KDE.
Apply spatio-temporal point-pattern methods and interpret their outputs.

title: Hands-on Exercise 6
text:
Analysis workflow

Import and validate the study-area boundary.
Clean event coordinates, dates, and temporal attributes.
Explore how event counts and locations change over time.
Estimate and compare spatio-temporal density surfaces.
Interpret persistent, emerging, and changing concentrations with appropriate caveats.







Temporal aggregation can change the apparent pattern, so the selected time unit should match the analytical question.

title: ISSS608 Visual Analytics and Applications
text:
This portfolio documents my hands-on work for ISSS608 Visual Analytics and Applications. It brings together geospatial data handling, thematic mapping, spatial point-pattern analysis, and spatio-temporal analysis using R.
Use the Hands-on Exercises dropdown in the navigation bar, or select an exercise below.

title: ISSS608 Visual Analytics and Applications
text:
Hands-on exercises


Exercise 1
Geospatial Data Science with R
Import, inspect, project, wrangle, and analyse spatial data with sf and the tidyverse.


Exercise 2
Thematic Mapping and GeoVisualisation
Build static and interactive thematic maps and complement them with statistical graphics.


Exercise 4
First-order Spatial Point Patterns
Explore nearest-neighbour analysis and kernel density estimation for spatial events.


Exercise 5
Second-order Spatial Point Patterns
Study spatial interaction across distances with G-, F-, K-, and L-functions.


Exercise 6
Spatio-temporal Point Patterns
Analyse how event intensity and spatial patterns change over time.








Each exercise page follows the corresponding course chapter and provides a dedicated place for the worked analysis, interpretation, and outputs.
